title: Another one I missed, which got an honorable mention in my “shortest ...
transcript: What are some plays or musicals with titles that have unusual properties? I'm curious to hear your examples, but I do have a bunch of my own, starting on the more basic side with some uncommon punctuation, like the brackets for [title of show] Parentheses like in the show (pray) from a few years ago. Quotation marks for jeremy o'haris's play “Daddy” This one doesn't really count cause it's only stylised this way in the marketing materials, not anywhere else that the title is listed out officially. But I did think it was funny that the 2016 revival of the Crucible has a period at the end of the title, which is like… …what does that mean? Also, if you've ever heard of the playwright debbie tucker green, she does this thing where all of the titles of her plays are completely in lowercase, and even her sort of stage name or her professional name as a writer is just her name, but always all lowercase. Also, we have Eisa Davis's recent play about a group of teenage musicians, and I had been calling this “Girl's Chance Music” but actually in music notation, those symbols indicate that you should be repeating everything within those brackets. So it's actually girls, girls chance chance music music. This is probably the only play I can think of that uses music notation in the official title. I also did a couple videos last year about the shortest and longest titles of plays that I've seen And as I said in that video, the shortest was the play 8 by Dustin Lance Black, which, unlike the musicals at Six or Nine, is just written out with the numeral 8. And then, as I said, by far the longest title was Jen Silverman's play Collective Rage, A play in five Betty's, in essence, a queer and occasionally hazardous exploration; Do you remember when you were in middle school and you read about Shackleton and how he explored the Antarctic?; Imagine the Antarctic as a p*ssy And it's sort of like that. Also, while we're here, going back to unusual punctuation, this might be the only play I can think of with a semicolon in its title, and it actually has 2. And definitely the only play with a semicolon and a question mark back to back. But I can also think of a couple that play around with what alphabet they're even using. This was a play from a few years ago about a Chinese production of Death of a Salesman. The title essentially means death of a salesman, but it's a mix of Mandarin and English. So the bilingual title of the play is, And I'm gonna butcher this, I'm sure, but I believe it was something like Salesman之死. And finally, we also had Gelsey Bell's musical MƆɹNIŊ [Morning//Mourning] And it was a double meaning of morning and mourning. But because these are homophones, she chose to write the title in the International Phonetic Alphabet. What are some other examples like this?
